answer.rationale: The core claims are a four-phase description of tool development (Purpose, Prototyping, Praxis, Post-project continuity) and a heuristic contrast between project-focused and user-focused approaches. Both rest on 22 interviews across 14 projects. The revision fixes the main transparency gaps reviewers raised. It adds an axial-coding step. The interview guide and coding tree are now actually supplied (A01–A04), and the coding tree maps codes onto the four phases. A scope statement on generalisability now appears in Methods. Saturation is now defined thematically. Concrete post-project examples are added. The typology is softened to non-exclusive 'predominant rationales'. Several residual problems remain. No project-by-approach mapping is given, so the claim that 'the majority' of projects were project-focused cannot be traced in the materials, and the coding tree has no codes for the two approaches. The added post-project examples mostly show exploration rather than realised uptake. The authors' own CLEVERFOOD involvement is disclosed as the sampling rationale but not reflected on as positionality. These weaken the typology as an empirical finding and call for more cautious wording. They do not undermine the descriptive phase model, and the typology is already framed as heuristic. I therefore judge the revision acceptable with caveats. R1's requests to publish 'lines of code' and to build a stakeholder-theory/open-innovation section were reasonably declined, because they rest on a misreading of qualitative 'codes' and are not needed for the study's aim.

issues.issue: The analytic procedure was unclear: open coding only, with no account of how codes were integrated into the phases, and no coding materials shared.
issues.response_claim: The authors say they used manual thematic coding with no ML or quantification, added an axial-coding second cycle, and provided the coding tree and interview guide.
issues.observed_change: The Methods now describe a second, axial cycle and cite OSF datasets. Supplement A02/A04 shows a coding tree that groups codes into Purpose, Process, Praxis and Post-project legacy. A01/A03 provide the interview guide.

issues.issue: The project-focused vs user-focused typology is a headline result, but projects are never assigned to approaches. R2 also found the categories too binary.
issues.response_claim: The authors agree the approaches are non-exclusive and add a clarifying sentence. They decline a matrix or schematic, citing Tables 2–3.

issues.issue: It was unclear how saturation was assessed across a heterogeneous sample of sectors and tool types, and whether findings are sector-specific.
issues.response_claim: The authors say saturation was assessed on process themes, not on sector or tool type. They report no meaningful sector differences and add a generalisability caveat to Methods.
issues.observed_change: A sentence defining thematic saturation was added. A Methods caveat says findings 'might not be fully generalisable'. Saturation is still reported per coder (10/11 interviews), with no comparative evidence shown across sectors or tool types.

evidence_limits: Interview transcripts are not available, so I cannot check whether coded excerpts support the phase model or the typology. The judgement relies on reported procedures, quotes, and the supplied coding tree and guide.
Supplements A02/A04 (coding tree) are images only, with no code definitions or example coded excerpts, so code-level dependability cannot be verified.
The manuscript says the interview guide is 'included in Appendix 2' and also hosted on OSF. Only the supplied attachments were reviewed; whether an in-paper appendix exists cannot be confirmed.
Under the task rules, no external sources or later reviewer outcomes were consulted.
